nameStory: Green rockcress gets its name from its love of rocky places and its membership in the rockcress genus. Though officially called Missouri rockcress in some guides, "green rockcress" better describes what you'll encounter in New England - a modest green plant that thrives in the cracks and crevices of rocky woodlands.
description: Green rockcress is a slender, upright biennial that grows from a cluster of lobed basal leaves. In spring, it sends up stems topped with delicate sprays of small, creamy-white flowers that look like tiny four-petaled crosses. The whole plant has a neat, orderly appearance, rarely getting much taller than knee-high, and often shows attractive reddish tints on its stems.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers with four petals arranged in a cross shape, clustered in elongated sprays at stem tips. Petals are noticeably longer than the small green sepals beneath them.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Basal leaves form a rosette and are deeply lobed like a dandelion leaf, persisting through the flowering season. Stem leaves are narrow, upright, and densely packed, often overlapping like roof shingles.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect, unbranched stems rise from a basal rosette, giving the plant a neat, formal appearance. Stems often show attractive reddish coloring, especially toward the base.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops narrow, upright seed pods (siliques) that split open when ripe to release small seeds. The pods follow the same orderly arrangement as the flowers.

habitat: Look for green rockcress in rocky or sandy woodlands, especially on bluffs and slopes with acidic soil. It favors spots where the forest floor is broken by exposed rock or sandy patches, often in partial shade beneath deciduous trees.

seasonality.spring: Prime blooming season with creamy-white flower clusters appearing in late spring. Fresh green basal leaves are prominent and stems begin their upward growth with reddish tints.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and narrow seed pods develop. Stem leaves remain dense and upright, while basal leaves may start to yellow as the plant focuses energy on seed production.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods split open to release seeds, and the aerial parts of the plant die back. New basal leaf rosettes may begin forming for next year's growth cycle.
seasonality.winter: Only the roots remain alive underground in established plants, while new seedlings may show small basal leaf rosettes if conditions are mild.

funFact: Despite being called Missouri rockcress, this plant is so rare and scattered across its range that finding one in New England is like discovering a botanical treasure - with only 19 recorded observations in the entire region, you're more likely to spot a rare bird than this elusive wildflower!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with smooth rockcress, but green rockcress has densely packed, overlapping stem leaves (versus widely spaced ones) and persistent basal leaves that stay green during flowering. Remember: "Green rockcress grips its leaves" - both basal and stem leaves stick around and cluster tightly.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "missouriensis" refers to Missouri, where this plant was first scientifically described, but don't let that fool you into thinking it's common there - this species has one of the most fragmented ranges of any North American wildflower, appearing in scattered pockets from New England to the Southeast with huge gaps in between.
compareHints: Green rockcress stands out from its relatives by its tidy, organized appearance and persistent basal leaves. Unlike smooth rockcress which has sparse, widely-spaced stem leaves, green rockcress packs its stem leaves densely together in an overlapping pattern. The related sicklepod produces distinctively curved seed pods, while green rockcress keeps its pods straight and upright like tiny soldiers in formation.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Smooth rockcress differs from its genus relatives sicklepod and Green rockcress primarily by its smooth, waxy-coated stem and shorter white petals.

Sicklepod differs from smooth rockcress by its distinctively curved seed pods (smooth rockcress has straight, upright pods) and its preference for rocky, mountainous habitats rather than disturbed soils.
